vignette:
He is a 46-year-old African man who comes across as careful, composed, and tired in a way that seems to go beyond ordinary stress. Before the event that changed his life, he describes himself as a man who took pride in order. As a curriculum designer, he spends his days shaping lessons, sequencing ideas, and thinking several steps ahead for other people's children. He has always preferred structure, and his wife often teased him for making grocery lists for the weekend. That preference for predictability now feels less like a personality quirk and more like something he clings to in order to keep himself steady.

The traumatic event happens during an encounter with police that begins as confusing and escalates quickly into terror. He had assumed he was doing something routine, something that would be resolved with a few questions. Instead, the officers' tone sharpens, voices rise, and the situation turns threatening in a matter of moments. He remembers the sound of commands, the hard look on the officers' faces, and the sense that reason no longer matters. What stays with him most is not one single image but the feeling of powerlessness: that his body is standing there while his mind is trying to understand how he has become a suspect, how he has become someone to be controlled. He reports being humiliated, frightened, and unable to speak clearly enough to explain himself. In the days after, he is startled by how quickly a normal afternoon can become a moment that he cannot leave.

Afterward, he tries to return to work as if nothing has happened. On paper, he remains functional. He attends meetings, revises lesson plans, and answers emails. But colleagues notice that he is quieter and more rigid. He begins checking his phone repeatedly during the day, not because anything is expected, but because he needs proof that he is still connected to the outside world. He avoids driving near the area where the encounter happened. If he sees police vehicles in traffic, his chest tightens and his hands go damp on the steering wheel. He catches himself scanning uniforms, exits, and faces in public spaces, automatically calculating where he could move if something happened again. He does not call this fear at first; he calls it awareness, then vigilance, then "just being careful."

At home, the change becomes harder to hide. His wife notices that he jumps when the front gate bangs or when someone knocks too hard. He starts sleeping lightly and wakes at the smallest sound. Some nights he lies still, listening to the house settle, convinced that if he relaxes even briefly, something bad will happen. Other nights he wakes from vivid dreams in which he is back in front of the officers, unable to make them listen. In the dream, his voice is either missing or coming out wrong, as though he is trying to speak underwater. When he wakes, he is drenched in sweat and angry at himself for not being able to shake it off.

He becomes more irritable, especially with his family, and then feels ashamed almost immediately. A harmless question from his wife can sound like pressure. A request from his teenage son can feel like one more demand on a system already straining to hold itself together. He sometimes leaves the room rather than risk snapping. Later, he sits alone and thinks about how unfair it is that the event did not end when the officers walked away. It follows him into breakfast, into the car, into meetings, into the silence of the evening. He describes feeling as though a part of him remains back in that encounter, still bracing for what will happen next.

He also notices how much he avoids talking about it. When friends ask how he is doing, he gives brief, polished answers and changes the subject. As a curriculum designer, he is skilled at turning complicated material into something neat and teachable; now he uses that same skill to make his own life look orderly from the outside. But privately, concentration has become harder. He rereads the same paragraph multiple times. He loses his train of thought in meetings. He sits down to plan a project and suddenly realizes he has been staring at the screen without absorbing anything. The effort of holding himself together leaves him exhausted.

Over time, he begins to understand that the event has altered the way he moves through the world. He does not feel safe in the way he once did, especially around authority or in situations where he cannot easily leave. He remains deeply attached to his wife and children, but even with them he feels a distance he cannot fully explain. He describes himself as living "on the edge of things," always prepared for the next wrong turn. The fear is not dramatic anymore; it is woven into daily life, shaping where he goes, how he sleeps, how closely he watches other people, and how long it takes before he can let his shoulders drop at the end of the day.
